In the absence of the Prime Minister, I will address my question to the Minister of Finance. My questioning centres on a newly-disclosed missile from our friend, John Turner, entitled "The Road Ahead".
In his September 22 epistle, Mr. Turner describes his attitude with regard to what transpired following the Bonn conference. In the letter, Mr. Turner points out that he feels that upon the Prime Minister's return to Canada, his insistence is going ahead unilaterally with his August 1 statement undermined cabinet ministers and got rumours running about who is in charge. Does the Minister of Finance feel he has been
December 21, 1978

undermined due to the Prime Minister's unilateral action since his return from meeting Helmut Schmidt in Bonn?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not feel like a man who has been undermined. The way in which the budget was received by the business community is proof that the management of the economy is all right. speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
My question also is directed to the Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker. I am sure the hon. gentleman knows that historically Canada has always enjoyed a strong position and reputation in international circles for the role it plays in the development of economic policy, particularly Bretton Woods and the International Monetary Fund.
Oral Questions
Would the minister tell us if it was his department which advised the Prime Minister of Canada to make the commitment, not only for the government but for all Canadians, at Bonn for a 5 per cent rate of growth in Canada during the course of the next year to help theThird World countries, when it was clearly evident to almost everyone in Canada that we had no opportunity whatsoever of fulfilling that commitment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when we were at Bonn it was in the context of a decision by many countries to try to stimulate western world economies. Of course we wanted to do our part and we wanted to stimulate our own economy as much as we could. That is why we have proposed measures to place the Canadian economy on a good footing. In fact, we are doing well in comparison with others. This year we will have a record trade surplus. There is a big increase in our consumer spending and our job creation program. If all the other countries could contribute as much as we are at this time, I am sure we would all be better off.

1 think the hon. gentleman misunderstood the import of my question. Very simply, it is that at Bonn-and the Prime Minister made this statement-we were not observers; we made commitments. The commitment which was given to the nations of the world was that we would benefit by a 5 per cent rate of real growth during the course of the next year. We now know that it will be around 3.3 per cent.
I ask the minister two questions. First, why would the Prime Minister of Canada, on the advice of his ministers, put Canada in the invidious position of making a commitment which could not, and cannot, be fulfilled and which it was known at the time could not be fulfilled, thereby lowering the credibility of Canada in the eyes of all the other economic ministers in the world?
Second, what does the Minister of Finance intend to tell the Prime Minister to say to Mr. Schmidt at the conference after Christmas? How will he explain why, having made a commitment in August, we have to renege on it in December because the growth rate has been only 3.3 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last July, when we were in Bonn, we merely told our colleagues who attended that meeting that we expected the rate of growth to be 5 per cent at the time when I brought down my budget barely two months before. Since then, the world economy has suffered many setbacks, such as the fall of the American dollar, the increase in interest rates as a result of the devaluation of the American dollar, and other factors such as those which have slowed down our own economy. I feel that we cannot isolate Canada from current world problems.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not ending the program. The advantages of the program are to continue. speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, December 19, consideration of Bill C-14, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, and motion No. 1 (Mr. Leggatt).

Mr. Speaker, I must say that many things have happened since I began my speech on Tuesday evening. The government has introduced closure on Bill C-14 and has then decided to restrict the time allowed to
us and perhaps even to prevent some members from making representations on behalf of their constituency.
First I would like to recall a statement which the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) made on September 1, 1978. At that time, the minister explained one of the major objectives of the new amendments to the unemployment insurance legislation. He said: I want to make sure that the unemployment insurance system fully encourages Canadians to look for a job and accept one. I must admit that I agree with those fine ideas but I must also point out that in practice, the minister seems to have forgotten his statement.
It has been said that the money the government will save through these cuts in unemployment insurance benefits will be used for job creation. In my riding the budget for Canada Works has been cut in half this year. Is that job creation? Is that using the money you save to create jobs? Over two years, the reduction will be about $1.5 billion, I think. That reduction represents about 60 per cent of the budget for the so-called economic boost of Canada.
The minister had announced a budget reduction of some $2.5 billion, but because of that federal budget cut, because of that 60 per cent reduction in unemployment benefits, a reduction which is detrimental to low income earners, to those who have less than all others, the federal government passes its responsibility over to the provincial governments which will have to pay these sums through their own social welfare or social assistance programs. People do not live without money, like apples in the trees. The minister says he wants to encourage people to find jobs. I agree with him on that, but at the present time there are about 900,000 people unemployment and only 50,000 jobs available. What can people do? Are they going to divide the jobs by 20 so that everybody can work? Are they going to create enough jobs to find work for everybody on the labour market? I do not think so, especially with a government such as this. The government will say that the provinces are responsible for the present situation. The provinces will have to increase further their taxes to cover the increase in their social assistance and social welfare expenses. These measures will again pit the provinces against the federal government.

December 21, 1978
Unemployment Insurance Act
Moreover, they have decided to reduce unemployment insurance benefits from 66% per cent to 60 per cent. Once again the people who have the smaller incomes will have to pay more. They will get 6% less in benefits and have to cope with an 8.6 per cent rate of inflation, so that their purchasing power will be reduced by 15 per cent. Are they going to keep on penalizing the meek who need help most?
Ever since I was elected to the House, most of the bills which have been introduced have been detrimental to the poor. This bill is a fine example of this. The unions have denounced this bill. I feel the CSD has clearly expressed my point of view when it said that through this bill and specifically clause 1, the government was penalizing everybody. It was assumed that Quebec workers would rather work than be unemployed and I do believe so too. Second, the federal government must create conditions that will help to create jobs. That is not what it is doing today. Third, the federal government ought to make an all-out attempt to see that workers do not suffer from the closing down of businesses. I think an effort has to be done in that area too. Fourth, the federal government must stop making cuts in its social programs.
That is the opinion of the CSD, a union from where I come from. But the CSD is not the only one that made representations. People in my riding, in cities like Saint-Flavien, Dos-quet, Victoriaville and Warwick did send me letters, did make representations so I would rise against this bill which penalizes people. We certainly are not against the fact that cheaters ought to be penalized, we are not against turning down those who abuse the system. But like the Economic Council of Canada, we recognize that four out of five persons who draw unemployment insurance do so because they have no choice. Only a minority of people abuse the system and not the majority of them.
And now they have decided to penalize the majority because of a particular small group. In the administration of all our social legislation, if not all our legislation, we see people who try to cheat. But are we going to change all this legislation? Are we going to make it still more restrictive and penalize the good? I say this on the basis that the good should not pay for the bad inside the system. We should have guidelines, we should have all kinds of possibilities to make our legislation applicable, to prevent cheating as much as possible, but to give all those who are really eligible the social advantages we have.
Furthermore, we are going to penalize our seasonal workers because it will be necessary to have 20 weeks of insurable employment to be able to receive unemployment insurance benefits. In my area there are construction workers who are going to find it difficult to accumulate 20 weeks of employment because of bad weather in winter and of a decline in the construction industry. There are also in my area clothing industries, a very disturbed, and even menaced sector, which does not give employment 12 months a year, unfortunately. The majority of the workers in that industry are women. It will

be difficult for those women to meet the requirement of 20 weeks of insurable employment.
We are told that exceptions will be made in areas which will show an unemployment rate lower than 11.5 per cent according to Statistics Canada. There, one will be eligible for unemployment benefits after having worked a lesser number of weeks. But because of these new provisions, a lot of these unemployed people who collect benefits will be dropped off the rolls. There will be no more areas where the unemployment rate will be 11.5 per cent; it will be impossible. They will disappear from the statistics. We know that as of now the statistics are misleading. They say: in your area you have approximately a 12 per cent to 13 per cent rate of unemployment. But that does not mean 12 per cent to 13 per cent unemployed. It does not take into account people on welfare people who have basic needs. Are we just going to say: As for you, you may starve to death. Our social laws no longer apply to you. You are no longer entitled to unemployment benefits. They will have to turn to welfare where there will be hassles, where one will have to kneel in order to try and get something. We have now reached that stage.
Here we are faced with a callous government which does not remember what it is to have a heart, to think of the underprivileged, to think of all the people of Canada who have to be able to live. To me these cuts are not the answer. Women are penalized and we know that in every piece of social legislation they are always the ones hardest hit. Women are penalized as well as young people who are out of school and looking for a job without finding one. Why? Because there are none. The labour market seems to have reached the saturation point, and no new jobs are being created.
In my own riding of Lotbiniere in the last year alone it would be easy to count on the fingers of one hand how many new industries did settle in the area. This is not due to a lack of manpower but to a lack of purchasing power on the part of the people. And now a little more of their purchasing power is being whittled down. The sale of our products will be made a little more difficult.
Go and see them!

An hon. member from the other side tells me to go and see them. I do not think that the Montreal area is in a much better position, not that there is no unemployment there.
I think that unemployment is now a national problem. I think that when we are close to the million mark, when there are almost one million unemployed, a responsible government must of necessity confront the problem and take some action in order to help the people.
This piece of legislation seeks to eliminate swindlers. I agree with that and, as I said a moment ago, I am prepared to help the government get rid of swindlers, but some people in my
December 21, 1978

riding come to see me every week because they have problems with the unemployment insurance, because of the deliberate attempt of some officers to get them out of the system and blame it on the computer, telling them their file has been "set aside" and their cheque might come in four weeks.
People are sick of the present system. Therefore, what will it be like with the new legislation? I regularly defend people with job problems before the arbitration board. Very often, we have to go before the board while the people are perfectly right and the officials could give them their benefits immediately. But they would rather say: Go and see your member of parliament, he will take care of it. In your case, you are lucky, your member of parliament is a Social Crediter. Those people like cases of unemployment. They can deal with them.
In the constituency of Lotbiniere, I replaced a man who had done a great job for the entire population and who was thoroughly devoted to the interests of his constituents. I represent the same people and I want to do the same job and always defend the weak, those who need it, the clothing or furniture plant employees, the unemployed, the welfare recipients, those who most need someone humane from their own constituency to serve them and to defend them from this type of bureaucracy.
As for the legislation under consideration, that we shall be forced to pass because of closure, and I am thinking about the bill on unemployment, certain members could have stood up and said something. Last Tuesday, certain government members rose in the House and said that the bill was not very good and would cause problems in their area because of the unemployment figures. I cannot wait to see what these people will do when it is time to vote. Will they truly represent their constituents or will they decide that they must first support their government? I believe that since we are elected by the people, whatever the legislation before us, we should vote according to our conscience and according to what the people whom we represent want us to do.
I know that we do not have much time and I would like as many members as possible to speak about the amendments. There are about 16 amendments to be discussed from now until 9.45, and we certainly do not have enough time to make the necessary representations.
I believe that each member should have the opportunity to say at least a few words about this bill. I shall therefore close my comments by saying that it is essential to change our present systems concerning unemployment and all other social legislation and to implement a universal guaranteed annual income, which would avoid the need for the ministers to rise in the House to say that we must put an end to abuse.
No abuse would be possible as everybody would get it. We would just have to get it back in some other way from those who already have an adequate income. I think we should give everyone a minimum income, an adequate income, so that they
Unemployment Insurance Act
will not have to go down on their hands and knees before some civil servant that will crush them a little further down and say: I have a good job, I am paid every week, I do not need you and you will get your cheque when I please.
So I hope, Mr. Speaker, that my remarks will be heard by the Minister of Employment and Immigration and that he will at least make up his mind to withdraw this bill and to improve the unemployment insurance legislation for the sake of all Canadian citizens.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This bill comes to us at this late stage in what really has been a parade of incompetence by this government. First, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced last August that he had suddenly discovered restraint. A month after that this minister got up-

Someone asked why I was not here for the vote yesterday evening. I had a good reason. I was away in the interest of national unity, since I was taking part in a program recorded in French designed to inform Quebeckers of the policies of the Conservative party, as it is obvious that only our party is able to keep our country united. We need the support of French Canadians. This is what I was doing yesterday evening. That is why I was not here to vote, but I will be here often for votes and I doubt very much that the members opposite will often be in the House after the next election.

We have had a veritable parade of incompetence. First, the Prime Minister discovered restraint in August. Then the minister discovered the need for this bill in September, but he was not able to bring it before this House for two full months. What is clear about that delay is that although the government should have been preparing this legislation and putting it together carefully over the summer, it was not because members of the government did not know that they had discovered restraint until they heard the announcement on August 1. That came as a total surprise to them. Consequently, they did not undertake the preparation they should have if they were going to put last summer to good use. If they had put last summer to good use and if they had been serious about introducing amendments which would have saved money and reduced inequity, they would have brought in a very different bill from the bill with which we are dealing in the House now.
This bill is designed to pretend restraint. It is not at all designed to achieve restraint. The bill is badly drafted. The Economic Council of Canada warned against this approach to this problem before the bill was introduced.
The ten provinces of Canada, including the one Liberal province-by one seat-the province of Prince Edward Island, and all the other provinces unanimously warned against this approach. Even the one NDP province warned against this approach during committee stage.
Quebec too.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And the province of Quebec-

-the province of Quebec where they have reservations with respect to this bill along with all other provinces because this is not an effective bill which can meet the objectives contemplated by the ministers, on the one part, or by other Liberal members, on the other part.

I must give particular credit to my colleagues the new member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan), the hon.

member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), and others who have proposed very serious improvements and reforms with which unfortunately the House of Commons will not be able to deal because this government is so concerned about support among its own members that it has introduced closure to cut off debate and stop parliament from carrying out the work of reform which parliament is here to carry out.
What is worse than this parade of incompetence is that the minister refuses to accept improvements, and for one reason: He did not propose those improvements. He would rather take credit for a bad bill than share credit for a good bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Absolute nonsense.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That contempt for parliament which is evident in the minister's rejection of amendments which would improve this legislation was also made absolutely clear when he deliberately and knowingly went ahead with the publication in the Canada Gazette of provisions in this legislation before this parliament had an opportunity to pass upon those provisions.
The minister will be hearing more about that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As my colleague the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) says, the minister will be hearing more about that, as will his colleagues, particularly from Atlantic Canada and les regions de l'Est du Quebec. They will also be hearing a great deal more about the minister's comment when he deliberately went out of his way to attack a generation of people in Canada, to attack a region of this country and to attack those who live in areas of high unemployment and who are not able to move. He attributed to them the basest of motives for being in a situation which is largely the creation of this government because of its failure in economic policy.
There is no question at all that the unemployment insurance program of this country very much needs reform. It costs much more that it should. It builds in a disincentive to work. It encourages too many Canadians in this land not to seek to develop their own potential. It includes serious invitations to abuse. The question I have to raise-and indeed the question will be raised across this country whenever an election comes-is why will the Government of Canada not take the time which parliament is here to give to improve this bill? Why does the government force this matter through, simply to save itself from embarrassment because its own members disagree? Why does the government force this bill through and not allow us an opportunity to consider and debate specific, positive reforms which would save more money and which would have other beneficial effects? Why docs the government not want to consider the reforms proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra and others in this House.
We know that this is the sixth or seventh bill in eight years dealing with the unemployment insurance question. It will not be the last one because the bill will create new injustices and it will require further changes later on. What is absolutely unacceptable to us on this side of the House is that the Government of Canada is forcing a bad bill through parlia-
December 21, 1978

ment. The bill is not bad by accident or because the government does not know better. The government is proceeding deliberately, and it is refusing to consider reforms which, first, would save the people of Canada more money; second, would be much more just to Canadians across the country; third, would create much more incentive to work among Canadians; and finally, would be much less complicated than this bill.
There are two essential differences between the two serious parties in this House on questions relating to unemployment insurance legislation. The first is that the government pretends that every unemployed Canadian is the same. By contrast, we recognize that hardship is much greater for those unemployed Canadians who have dependants for whom they have to care, and we recognize also that abuse has been much greater among those Canadians who do not have dependants for whom they have to care. The other difference is that the government's proposal is very complicated. It establishes different standards based upon different regions of the country. [Translation]
We heard the other night the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Lapointe) who referred to the problems caused in his own riding by an artificial line drawn by this government. There are now in the riding of Charlevoix and many other ridings in the province of Quebec small villages on one side of the Saguenay river with a standard and other small villages on the other side of the river with a different standard. So this is a double-standard government.
It is absolutely unacceptable to us to have this kind of situation brought in by this government, creating confusion and complexity where none needs to be. We would base the distinction which must be brought into this bill on whether or not an unemployed Canadian has to support other persons. The government, in contrast, bases its distinction on whether the unemployed live in Canada, on what side of the Saguenay they are. If they are on one side of the Saguenay river, they are treated one way; if, by sheer chance, they happen to be on the other side, they are treated another way.
That is absolutely absurd. It is bureaucratic nonsense imposed in a way that is guaranteed to create injustice in this country, and yet that is precisely what this government is proposing. They are proposing it despite the fact there is a better way, because they know there is before the House of Commons right now amendment No. 14 proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, which is a much better approach which will not create the problems which are being created by the government's own proposal.
The government's stubbornness is costing hundreds and probably thousands of Canadians simple equality and justice of treatment. It does not care about the people who suffer from the double standard, the people who, because they happen to live on one side of the Saguenay and not on the other, will be treated differently from their cousins or neighbours. It prefers to persist in its stubbornness and push through a bad bill rather than accept amendments which would make it better.
Unemployment Insurance Act
Our proposal, which has been outlined effectively by other members of the House, establishes that persons with dependants would continue to be covered for two-thirds of earnings for which they are now insured. We do that for a reason- because these are the Canadians who most need help in our system. It stands to reason that they need help most because they have more other Canadians to care for. Also, they are the Canadians who are least mobile. If you have dependants, it is not as easy to move to other places where you might find work as it is if you do not have dependants. These are people who have special cause for the attention and concern of their government, but their special requirements are absolutely ignored by this government.
Instead of dealing with people who have particular problems, this government has set up a little artificial group of districts in the country. It imposes a geographical complexity which ensures vested injustice being dealt to a large number of Canadians. We are proposing in the amendment introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, a two-tier system. It would introduce a second category of benefits based upon the principle that those Canadians who do not have dependants under the Income Tax Act will be covered for only 50 per cent of their earnings.
It has been made very clear by members on this side that we are also proposing, as part of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, that we will vest in a married couple the right to decide and establish themselves which one of the couple will be the one to whom dependants are attached. Because the law as it now stands involves a serious discrimination against women, and we propose a means by which that can be mitigated. That too this government have turned down. They would prefer to live with discrimination against women than to remove it as it exists in this bill.
The proposal for the two-tier system which we introduced would save, by the government's own reckoning, in the neighbourhood of $850 million. Their proposal, by their reckoning, would save in the neighbourhood of $935 million. But-and the buts are pretty important-it would add at least $43 million to the welfare costs of the provinces and Lord knows how much to the welfare costs of the municipalities across this country. It is unfortunately far too typical of the restraint that pretends to be practised by this government. They are not reducing over-all expenditure; they are simply making some paper cuts and passing the real burden on to other levels of government which cannot afford to bear them as well as the Government of Canada can.
I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Maine), who represents an Ontario constituency, shaking his head negatively.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister probably anticipated something I want to say later on about the yet unspecified costs to Canada of this bill introduced by the government. [English]
Because I am sure that one of the uncalculated costs to the people of Canada is that there will be a need for this government to pour more money into regions which have been treated by this bill. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The two-tier proposal we have put forward is a much better way of approaching the problem we face for a number of reasons. First, there will be a direct saving which is significantly more than the aggregate saving of the measures being forced down the throat of parliament by the government. Second, the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra will not create the number of problems which will have to be dealt with later, the problems that the government is ensuring will occur by the nature of its legislation. Those problems will turn out to be very expensive to the country, expensive not only in terms of the obstacles to hope and development which will be put in the path of individual Canadians, but also expensive in terms of new programs. Perhaps there will be additions to winter works, LIP and a number of programs which will come forward to deal with the problems the government is creating deliberately today in the House of Commons.
Our proposal has the advantage of being acceptable to all of the provinces and, I would judge, the municipalities of this country. The mere fact that a matter is acceptable to the provinces is cause enough for the government to oppose it.

That has been well established. That is why we have not achieved such a healthy state of unity during the ten years in which the government has been responsible for the direction of national affairs. The government goes out of its way to disagree with the provinces. The amendment we are putting forward is an amendment supported in its general thrust by the provinces, and would be far preferable to the provinces of Canada than the matter forced by closure down the throats of members of the House of Commons by the government today.
The proposal we are making would not create the bureaucratic nightmare which will be imposed upon the citizens of this country by the establishment of districts based upon geography where average levels of unemployment happen to be different. It would not create this nonsense where citizens, as a Liberal member said the other night, on one side of the Saguenay have a different set of standards from citizens on the other side of the Saguenay. It would not write in the law the kind of absurdity which is central to the bill before us now.
One of the very, very important reasons the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra is superior to the bill before the House is that it builds in a clear incentive for Canadians to go to work. It would reduce the percentage of benefits available to people in the second tier, people without dependants under the Income Tax Act. As I have indicated, these are the people who are more mobile. Perhaps the minister is disagreeing with his own statistics, but before doing so he had better see if he has published them in the Canada Gazette. Statistically these people have been indicated as being more likely to abuse the system.
The minister is sucking his finger.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, I notice the minister is sucking his finger. That fact is pointed out by the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir) who has suffered a double insult from the government. First of all, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) went to Cape Breton with his rather eccentric views on unemployment and the attitudes toward work of the citizens of Cape Breton. Now those people are maligned as simple thumbsuckers instead of working Canadians by the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
In the proposal we are putting forward there is a very real incentive to Canadians who do not have dependants to go out and work, those people who make up the mobile part of the Canadian work force.

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: What about married women?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister is talking about married women. Will the minister go so far, in his rush to closure and his rush to silence his own members, as to accept even that portion of our amendment that allows a family unit to determine which of their number will be categorized as the one to whom dependants attach? Or will he persist in the bill he introduced which continues discrimination against women?
The proposal of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra is a much better manner in which to deal with the problems posed

for Canada by the present unemployment insurance scheme. The government refuses to let parliament consider that better way. It wants to force through the House of Commons a bad, bad bill. It is a terrible abuse of parliament. We are here not just to talk; we are here to improve pieces of legislation. I admit that there have been occasions in the House when opposition has been sometimes negative and there have not been things to propose. This is not one of those times. This is a time when party has come forward with a very acceptable, clearly preferable means of solving this problem.
I cannot speak for members of the New Democratic Party. They speak often for themselves. They have not been proposing anything positive. Their amendments are consistently destructive ones.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Our amendments point out a much better way in which Canada can deal with the problems posed by the unemployment insurance system. It is a much better way, but the government refuses to allow the Parliament of Canada to consider amendments which would improve the bill. The government refuses to allow the Parliament of Canada to consider amendments which would save Canadians more money, which would build in more incentive to work, and which would have a number of other advantages to the people of the country.
The legislation before us is a terrible abuse of the unemployed, a terrible disservice to Canadians out of work. The particular bitterness of that is so many Canadians who are out of work are out of work because we have had a government which for a decade has failed to give priority to economic growth in the country. Consequently, we have a government that created the problem of unemployment, which is at the base of the costs of the unemployment insurance program.
This proposal which is being forced down the throat of parliament and the throats of Liberal backbenchers involves a terrible waste of taxpayers' money. The government is forgoing savings which would be available. Our proposals would save more money than the proposals the Government of Canada is putting forward now.
How many will go on welfare?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This proposal wastes money for the Canadian taxpayers, not simply because it forgoes the savings, but because, as I mentioned earlier, it creates significant new likelihoods of spending by this government. We know the government has problems with the hon. member for Charlevoix; and we have heard hon. members over there talk about this. We know the government has problems with the hon. member for South Western Nova, and we have heard members speak about that. We know that the government is having problems with the hon. member for Hochelaga, and we can sympathize in that regard.
The fact is that even if members over there are able to cause those people to be absent from the votes, or even if they are able to cause them to put party before principle, which, of course, is part of the reason that presumably they joined that party, they are still going to have to face the demands of those members and of countless other members whose interests in their constituents and in their provinces are being very seriously damaged by this bill.
What we are going to see-and no doubt this will be smuggled through in the estimates-are millions of dollars pumped into those areas where problems are being caused by this government with this bill. That money will be pumped in in an attempt to rescue the Liberal party, and pumped in perhaps ultimately to deal with new real problems that are being created by this bill; but which should have been dealt with in anticipation, and never have been caused by this government. No doubt we will see this government try to smuggle through this House in a new session millions of dollars-I cannot say hundreds of millions as I do not know how much, but certainly it will be millions of dollars-in new
expenditures to deal with the new problems that are being created. These are problems that do not now exist but which will come into being when this bill comes into law. That is the other way in which this bill is a terrible waste of the taxpayers' money in this country.
What we are seeing here today in this closure and in the reason for its introduction amounts to terrible treatment of the government's own principle. Because it is part of the tradition of this place, part of the history of parliament and part of what makes it work, that members of parliament, at least within their own parties, and preferably within this House of Commons, have the right to defend the interest of their constituents and their regions against legislation that is going to be harmful to those constituents and regions. They should at least have the right to put on record their defence. They should at least be given the right to get up and speak and to say: "Look what you are doing to the people of northern New Brunswick; look what you are doing to the people of Newfoundland; look what you are doing to the people of Prince Edward Island; look what you are doing to the people of Nova Scotia; look what you are doing to the people of eastern Quebec".
They should at least be given that right, but they are not being given that right. This government is denying the right of dozens of members to represent the interests of those who in their constituencies will be damaged by the imposition of closure. This imposition of closure is not to stop the opposition from speaking, but to stop the government's own members from talking.
Shame, shame!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The government can stop them from talking, but presumably some of them will want to vote. Let me give them a warning now. If by some accident they do not happen to be here, we will make it a point on the hustings to go into their constituencies and make clear that they were absent and did not stand up and be counted in the interests of their constituents when this government forced through a bad bill. We will be very interested in seeing how the hon. member for Charlevoix votes, how the hon. member for South Western Nova votes, how the hon. member for Hochelaga votes, how members from the north shore of New Brunswick vote, and how members from Newfoundland vote. We will be very interested in seeing whether they are going to put their party ahead of the interests of their regions, whether they are going to support this attempt to ram a bill down the throat of parliament when a better bill exists and when acceptable proposals for reform have been put forward by members on this side of the House. We will be interested to see how they vote, sir.
There is no question as to how we will vote. We will vote against this bill, and we will look forward to the earliest possible opportunity as a new government to bring in a better bill.
Hear, hear!

ly after the speech the hon. member has just made, and let me explain why I say that. I say that on the basis of the record of Hansard itself, which evidently he failed to read when he prepared his speech.

-I said that this bill was a step in the right direction-

Restraint and reform are sorely needed. We will see what happens to the amendments we put forth.
Then he concluded with this great statement of Tory policy:
We will see what happens to the amendments we put forth. Then we will make up our minds on the bill itself.
After 34 meetings of the committee, having heard all the witnesses and the amendments they have put forward, and there being, contrary to what the Leader of the Opposition said, ample opportunity in committee for this bill to be discussed, that hon. member on Monday in this House said:
Then we will make up our minds on the bill itself.

This bill is iniquitous. It is a bad bill, an unjust bill and an unfair bill. It is a bad bill, Mr. Speaker, and it is bad legislation.

To make it a better bill.

To make it a better bill, exactly. Let us see some cohesion and consistency over there. Until the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra changes his job he is the official spokesman for the official opposition on unemployment insurance, and he is the one who said that the bill is a step in the right direction. A small step, you fool.

The Leader of the Opposition went on to ask why we are forcing this bill through, as if there had not been ample opportunity for discussion in the committee. We did have ample opportunity. Members of the official opposition had ample opportunity to express their views in committee. Some, such as the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan) and the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), made a distinct effort to put forward an alternative view. We did not agree with it but we looked at it. To claim that the bill is being forced through after 34 committee meetings is stretching things too far. Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition would benefit from staying around here a little bit longer to find out what his colleagues are doing in committee. In making statements like that he is saying, in essence, that his colleagues have done nothing. That is not true. We have seen them work as hard as we did every day for five weeks.
The Leader of the Opposition also was very sarcastic about the geographic districts. Several times in his speech he made reference to one side of the Saguenay or the other side. I realize that he does not want to hear a critique of his speech because that is no fun and it is easier to criticize others. I do not blame him for engaging in conversations with another member at the present moment.
Let me remind the all-knowing Leader of the Opposition that it was the Tory party that introduced the idea of geographic districts in the discussion on Bill C-27. I believe the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) proposed it, but apparently it is no longer convenient so it is being attacked.
The Leader of the Opposition also put forward the grand scheme of the Tory party for a two-tier system, namely, that the unemployment insurance payments should differentiate between the head of a family and the secondary wage earner. There were extensive debates on this proposal in committee which are reported in the proceedings. The Tory party seems to ignore a number of facts. One is that heads of families or people alone without dependants have certain basic costs such as rent and heat which are virtually the same in both cases. Further, differentiating between the two groups would adversely affect women and young people.
Extensive studies carried out by the Unemployment Insurance Commission explained to members of the opposition- perhaps this was not reported to the Leader of the Opposition-that women without dependants make up 95 per cent of all women claimants of UIC benefits. Not only does the Tory party seem to ignore that fact, but they have engaged in a rather unusual policy approach whereby in one committee room certain members of their party defend women's rights and oppose anything that seems to be discrimination, while in another room other members of their party propose a differential in the benefits which would affect the very same women.

Another weakness of the two-tier proposal and a strong reason why we rejected it is that it introduced the idea of welfare or income transfer payments-in effect, an assessment of need. That is a poor basis on which to assess need since it would not take family income into consideration.

A point of order, Mr. Speaker. I just want to point out to the hon. member that it was not this party that introduced the concept of differentiating benefits on the basis of need. The government introduced it in amendments to this bill with respect to the charge back to high income families.

Mr. Speaker, we should not mix one with the other. The two-tier system proposed by the Conservative party has exactly this effect. Let us not mix this with the effect on high income groups because we are talking about what the net effect of the two-tier system would be.
The Leader of the Opposition refused to answer what I thought was a legitimate question by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). He wanted to know if the Leader of the Opposition would support the government if his amendment were defeated, which would still mean at least supporting a measure which would cut costs considerably. Of course, it was beneath the dignity of the Leader of the Opposition to reply, yet it went to the very heart of this bill.
As to the final, grandiose, theatrical challenge by the Leader of the Opposition to members on our side regarding whether they will show up for the vote on this bill, I should remind him of the dismal record of his party regarding other bills in this parliament when some members of the Tory party did not show up for the vote.
That is not true.

I remember occasions very clearly when members of the Progressive Conservative party-who may no longer be members-did not show up to vote on a bill similar to this. Instead of sounding so pure and righteous the Leader of the Opposition should perhaps examine the record of his party.
In the debate on Bill C-14 it seems to me that something has to be said about its impact and what will be done in 1979 to offset the changes it will bring about. It is important to record that in 1979, $710 million will be invested in our economy in different ways in order to create jobs. Of this, a cash expenditure of $570 million will go to direct job creation. Forgone tax revenue will account for $100 million and $40 million in unemployment insurance funds will be used for job creation. This strategy is supposed to create some 113,000 jobs for one year which will mean, as I understand it, a 70 per cent increase in job-creation funds over the current year.
Some elements of this program that will be put in place are, first, the employment tax credit program to assist businessmen in expanding employment and job seekers in getting work which will be improved. There will be $70 million provided exclusively for skill training. Twenty million dollars will be used for the development of measures to help industry overcome critical shortages of skilled people. This will be done in conjunction with the provinces, industry and labour. Twenty million dollars will be added to skill training in and by industry. Thirty million dollars will be used to cover the institutional costs of increased skill training for industry
A portable wage subsidy will be introduced to spur the re-employment of people laid off as a result of economic shifts and support. The youth employment program will be carried out at a cost of $225 million in the next year. Its major component is job experience training, commonly known as the JET program. This will provide employment and work experience for over 63,000 young Canadians. We will be utilizing unemployment insurance benefits, in the case of those who are eligible for them, to cover the $1.50 an hour wage subsidy involved in this program. In the case of those who are not eligible for unemployment insurance, the government will provide the subsidy in total.
The summer youth employment program funds and the year-round youth employment and the employability program funds will be increased from $14.5 million in fiscal 1978-79 to nearly $110 million in fiscal 1979-80.
It will also be desirable to have a look at what areas the government might wish to monitor as possible areas where amendments to this bill might be required to see that certain distortions might not take place in our general social and economic pattern. For instance, I would be interested in seeing the effect of the bill monitored and the effect it will have on entry and re-entry qualification for benefits. If this should cause a movement of people from rural to urban areas because people would be better able to re-enter the labour force when running out of benefits, then, of course, we would want to monitor this movement very closely. Trends of this kind which could lead to further centralization, urbanization or abandonment of rural areas are not desirable in any nation and we do not want to see that develop under any circumstance.
I would also be interested, as would many members of this House, in monitoring the effect of the reduction of the allowance for manpower training from the $45 which is being paid to the proposed $10 a week per person payable to the person who is not the primary wage earner. If it were to be established that this would have an adverse effect, then we should see to it that the allowance is brought back to the original level.
I would also like to say a few words about a widespread practice in urban Canada where more and more employers are requesting their employees to put in overtime. In the city where I come from we see this pattern, and I suspect this is not an isolated occurrence. The practice of demanding more and more time in my opinion is a bad one. It is a bad practice for health and safety reasons. This has been proven on a number of occasions by studies carried out by various jurisdictions. It is bad practice because it keeps unemployed people waiting for jobs for longer periods of time. It is a bad practice because it affects the job growth rate negatively. I would urge the

December 21, 1978

Unemployment Insurance Commission to do whatever it can to discourage this practice of overtime work and to exert every possible pressure on employers to see that it comes to an end. However, I realize that there are difficulties associated with that.
In his closing remarks the Leader of the Opposition made reference to the fact that the government has failed to give priority to economic growth in its policy. Let me remind the Leader of the Opposition that this government has been able to produce 250,000 to 380,000 jobs every year over the past seven or eight years because of its economic policies. This surely demonstrates that the government has done whatever it could to stimulate economic growth according to very sound principles.
With that, Mr. Speaker, I will leave the Leader of the Opposition to meditate on his own statements.

Mr. Speaker, in my first speech in the House, I had referred to the political and economic crisis in our country, the solution of which will have a deep influence on the future of Canada. That is why the members of this House are dealing at this time in our history with a bill which will have a major impact for all Canadians.
For this reason, I am quite pleased, Mr. Speaker, to take part in this debate which the government has tried to restrict. A motion for closure was introduced in the House of Commons as well as in committee. The members of our committee, the representatives of the people, were not even allowed to take part in the debate on the bill in committee. There are very few instances, Mr. Speaker, of such tactics being used by a party whose leader has advocated the popular policy of participatory democracy. It is a real human comedy, a plot which is still better than those of Moliere, a real masterpiece contrived by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
Any bill, Mr. Speaker, and any amendment is designed for a political purpose, that is to win the support of the majority of Canadians. They are all designed to make a good impression on Canadians in all regions, people of all social or economic classes, no matter what arguments, for or against, are presented during the debate, and that is done more particularly because we are getting closer every day to a general election. Mr. Speaker, there is no question about the fact that it is a controversial bill, not only so because members on both sides of the House do not agree on it, but also because members of the Liberal party do not agree among themselves, even though this does not show that much has or has not been said officially in the speeches we have heard in the House. But we all know very well that even the party in power is divided. It is quite natural, Mr. Speaker, that the actions taken by the Liberal party in this bill are political in nature and come as a reaction
Unemployment Insurance Act
to pressures from Canadians who ask for cuts in spending and that they are in the line of a philosophy of economic restrictions which prevails not only in Canada, but in the whole world.
But, Mr. Speaker, since the government is said to have the responsibility of answering the needs of the majority of the population, this bill should be devised in a humanitarian way and from the point of view of social morality and we do not see that in the bill. Yes, we are in favour of economic restrictions because of ten years of wastage under this government led by a "Trudeaucratic" party which is ill advised, as far as priorities are concerned, by an army of bureaucrats trying to overcome the economic crisis by increasing the army of unemployed and there was 1.308 billion unemployed, Mr. Speaker, according to the statistics for March of this year, including official and unofficial figures, thus a struggle which increases the army of people on welfare by adding 250 million unemployed deprived of benefits. That is a struggle of justice, a struggle called responsible in the restraint philosophy.
If you are looking for logic, Mr. Speaker, you will have much difficulty finding it. Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words on this clause. One involves the major change that has taken place through this amendment which will allow those who have something wrong with their gun to take it down to the gun shop to get it fixed. It is logical that if you do not need a licence to have the gun in the first place and you take it down to the gun shop to have it fixed, you should not need a licence to get it back again because nothing has changed except the fact that a bona fide gunsmith has repaired it.

They did not require an additional part or the modification of any part of the gun. It was a simple operation whereby one or two pieces were reversed, pieces which were already part of the gun, to make it into an automatic weapon. This means, of course, that we will have to pay attention to those whom we classify as bona fide gunsmiths.
We now have some difficulty in northern Ontario which has resulted from some hysteria in the department, and that department has a tendency to hysteria with regard to gun-running. To them all these guns can become dangerous weapons. As everyone knows, there are thousands of pseudo-machine guns around the country which were not considered to be fully automatic weapons because they were not used in that way, but some parts in most of them would allow them, with some modification, or in one case just the turning of one piece, to become fully automatic guns, and if you had a 30 to 60-shell clip, you had a viable machine gun.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I will make the remarks now which I attempted to make at second reading stage. The explanatory note states the following:
These amendments would ensure that the delivery of a firearm by the operator of a business that includes the manufacturing, buying or selling at wholesale or retail, importing, repairing, altering or modifying or taking in pawn of firearms to a person from whom he received it in the course of such business, and the receipt of the firearm by that person from the operator of the business, does not constitute an offence.
To summarize very briefly, when parliament passed the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1977, it intended that the acquisition of guns would be controled by the firearms acquisition certificate system. Parliament clearly intended that people do not need certificates in order to keep the guns they already own, but only when they undertake to acquire a gun. Indeed, paragraph 95(2)(b) of the Criminal Code exempts an individual from the requirement to produdce a certificate when his gun is being returned to him by an individual to whom it has been lent. Unfortunately, the law does not specifically exempt an individual from the requirement to produce a certificate when his gun is being returned to him by a licensed business dealer who has taken the gun into his possession for the purpose of repairing or storing it. An amendment to the legislation is
Criminal Code
urgently required before January 1, 1979, to provide such an exemption for several reasons.
Those reasons are brief, and they are three in number. Provinces have adopted different interpretations of the present law with the result that some jurisdictions will enforce the law and others will not. That is to say, at the present time I understand that some provinces under the present legislation will require the owner of a gun to have a firearms acquisition certificate before his gun can be returned to him, while other provinces will not enforce it.
There is a certain degree of business anxiety because even in jurisdictions where the law may not be enforced, businesses are concerned either that they may be prosecuted or that they will lose their business permits. Remington Ltd. is currently recalling more than 2,000 guns across the country for repair. In view of the inconsistent application of the law which might occur, Remington very probably will insist that individuals produce a certificate before the guns are returned to them.
Thirdly, having to do with safety considerations, some individuals, particularly in the case of the Remington recall, may not bother to have their guns repaired if they must produce a certificate in order to have them back. This could undermine their own or others safety, which is entirely in conflict with the intent of gun control.
In short, what I am saying is that there is a possibility of having different interpretations of the present law in different areas of the country, something we do not want to see occur. There is a certain amount of anxiety on the part of present owners of guns, including businessmen who may be in the business of repairing those guns, not knowing whether to request a firearms acquisition certificate for the return of a gun. As I say, for simple safety considerations we would not want to have any inconsistency or any doubt in anyone's mind; it should be clear that they are able to turn guns over to a manufacturer for restoration or repair and have them returned. We would not want them to feel that they should not put guns in for repair simply because they may be hassled, if you like, for a firearms acquisition certificate.
